name: Canaima National Park
blurb: Tepui plateaus, pitcher plants and the jaguar of the Gran Sabana.

tip.title: Thin out the ants
tip.text: Ants feed pitcher plants, frogs, anteaters and armadillos. Set Ants to -100% and follow the ripple up to the jaguar.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Savanna grasses and sedges
nodes.desc: Grasses and sedges cover the open Gran Sabana, growing on rocky, sandy, nutrient-poor soils derived from sandstone.

nodes.name: Miconia
nodes.desc: Berry-bearing shrubs and small trees among the most recorded plants around the park; GloBI records show bananaquits and tanagers eating their fruit.

nodes.name: Cecropia & other forest trees
nodes.desc: Forest fills the hollows and lines the rivers, supplying leaves, fruit and dead wood to sloths, tapirs, termites and bats.

nodes.name: Tepui pitcher plants
nodes.desc: Carnivorous plants of the tepuis that trap insects, mostly ants, in leaf pitchers to make up for scarce nutrients; many rely on bacteria to digest the prey.

nodes.name: Termites
nodes.desc: Feed on dead wood and plant litter, and are a main food of giant anteaters and giant armadillos.

nodes.name: Ants
nodes.desc: Abundant forest and savanna insects. They are the main prey caught by Heliamphora pitchers and a staple for anteaters, armadillos and frogs.

nodes.name: Red brocket
nodes.desc: A forest deer recorded near the park that browses leaves and eats fruit and fungi; prey for jaguars.

nodes.name: Lowland tapir
nodes.desc: A large browser and fruit-eater named among the Gran Sabana's mammals; a big prey animal for jaguars.

nodes.name: Linnaeus's two-toed sloth
nodes.desc: A slow leaf-eater of the canopy. In the harpy eagle article sloths are the most important prey group.

nodes.name: Seba's short-tailed bat
nodes.desc: The most recorded mammal in the GBIF data near the park. It eats fruit and helps spread seeds.

nodes.name: Bananaquit
nodes.desc: The most recorded bird near the park; a small nectar, fruit and insect eater that GloBI records feeding on Miconia fruit.

nodes.name: Palm tanager
nodes.desc: A common fruit-eating songbird; GloBI records show it eating Miconia fruit.

nodes.name: Bumblebee poison dart frog
nodes.desc: A small yellow-and-black frog of the Gran Sabana region that eats tiny insects, especially ants, on the forest floor.

nodes.name: Giant anteater
nodes.desc: Eats mostly ants and termites, dug from nests with its claws. Only jaguars and pumas are known to hunt adults.

nodes.name: Giant armadillo
nodes.desc: Eats mainly termites and ants, and its burrows are used by many other animals, making it a habitat engineer.

nodes.name: Black vulture
nodes.desc: One of the most recorded birds near the park; it feeds on carrion, helping return dead animals to the ecosystem.

nodes.name: Harpy eagle
nodes.desc: A huge forest eagle that hunts mostly tree-dwelling mammals, sloths above all, and sometimes young deer.

nodes.name: Jaguar
nodes.desc: The top predator of the park. It hunts large mammals such as tapirs and deer, and is one of the few animals known to hunt adult giant anteaters.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Powers the grasslands and forest; tepui summits are often wrapped in cloud.

nodes.name: Rain & tepui mist
nodes.desc: The Gran Sabana gets roughly 1,600 to 2,200 mm of rain a year, with a rainy season of about ten months.

nodes.name: Nutrient-poor sandstone soil
nodes.desc: Acidic soils from sandstone are low in nutrients, which shapes the stunted shrubs and the carnivorous plants.

nodes.name: Dark-water rivers
nodes.desc: Many Gran Sabana rivers are acidic and tea-colored from humic acids and tannins; forests line their banks.

nodes.name: Fungi, bacteria & litter fauna
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the thin soil.
